title: All 12 tenses
summary: Talk about the present, the past and the future with the right verb form.

lessons.title: Present Simple
lessons.explain: Use the present simple for habits, routines, facts and things that are always true. Use the base verb, and add -s or -es with he, she and it. Questions and negatives use do or does.
structures: Positive: Subject + base verb (+s): She works.
Negative: Subject + do/does not + base verb: She does not work.
Question: Do/Does + subject + base verb?: Does she work?
positive: I walk to school every day.
Water boils at 100 degrees.
My father works in a bank.
negative: I do not eat meat.
My father does not work on Sundays.
questions: Do you live near here?
Does the shop open at nine?
reallife: Describing a routine: I get up at six, and I take the bus at seven.
Giving facts: The museum closes at five.

mistakes.wrong: She don't like coffee.
mistakes.right: She doesn't like coffee.
mistakes.why: With he, she and it, use does not (doesn't).

mistakes.wrong: Does he works here?
mistakes.right: Does he work here?
mistakes.why: After does, the main verb stays in the base form.

exercises.why: My sister is she, so add -s.

options: Does she speaks French?
Does she speak French?
Do she speak French?

exercises.prompt: They ___ not like spicy food. (do / does)
Which sentence is about a fact?
options: The sun rises in the east.
The sun is rising now.
The sun rose early.
exercises.why: General truths use the present simple.

options: He go to work by bus.
He goes to work by bus.
He going to work by bus.
She doesn't likes tea.
She doesn't like tea.
She not like tea.

assessment.why: The bus is it, so add -s.

lessons.title: Present Continuous
lessons.explain: Use the present continuous for actions happening now, for temporary situations, and for arrangements in the near future. Form it with am, is or are and the verb with -ing.
structures: Positive: Subject + am/is/are + verb-ing: I am reading.
Negative: Subject + am/is/are not + verb-ing: He is not reading.
Question: Am/Is/Are + subject + verb-ing?: Are you reading?
positive: I am cooking dinner now.
They are staying with friends this week.
We are meeting Sara tomorrow.
negative: I am not watching TV.
She is not working today.
questions: What are you doing?
Is it raining?
reallife: On the phone: I am walking to the station. I will be there soon.
Small talk: Are you enjoying the course?

mistakes.wrong: I am knowing the answer.
mistakes.right: I know the answer.
mistakes.why: State verbs such as know, like and want are not normally used in the continuous.

mistakes.wrong: She is work now.
mistakes.right: She is working now.
mistakes.why: After is, the verb needs -ing.

options: He is runing.
He is running.
He is runs.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence describes a future arrangement?
options: I am meeting my boss on Friday.
I meet my boss every Friday.
I met my boss on Friday.
exercises.why: The present continuous can show a planned future event.

options: I am wanting a coffee.
I want a coffee.
I wanting a coffee.
Are you listen to me?
Are you listening to me?
Do you listening to me?

assessment.prompt: We ___ not working today. (am / is / are)

options: He is swiming.
He is swimming.
He is swimmming.

lessons.title: Present Perfect
lessons.explain: Use the present perfect to connect the past with now: experiences, recent events and things that started in the past and continue. Form it with have or has and the past participle. Do not use it with a finished time such as yesterday.
structures: Positive: Subject + have/has + past participle: I have seen it.
Negative: Subject + have/has not + past participle: I have not seen it.
Question: Have/Has + subject + past participle?: Have you seen it?
positive: I have visited Mysuru twice.
She has lived here since 2020.
They have just arrived.
negative: I have not finished my homework.
He has never eaten sushi.
questions: Have you ever been to Goa?
How long has she worked here?
reallife: In an interview: I have worked as a teacher for five years.
Asking about experience: Have you used this software before?

mistakes.wrong: I have seen him yesterday.
mistakes.right: I saw him yesterday.
mistakes.why: Yesterday is a finished time. Use the past simple.

mistakes.wrong: She has lived here since three years.
mistakes.right: She has lived here for three years.
mistakes.why: Use for with a period of time and since with a starting point.

options: She has went home.
She has gone home.
She has go home.
exercises.why: Gone is the past participle of go.

options: Have you ever tried Thai food?
Did you ever tried Thai food?
Have you ever try Thai food?
I have lost my keys.
I have lose my keys.
I has lost my keys.

assessment.prompt: She ___ in this company for ten years. (work)

options: I have met her last week.
I met her last week.
I have meet her last week.
assessment.why: Last week is a finished time.

assessment.prompt: They have lived here ___ ten years. (for / since)

options: Has he finished yet?
Have he finished yet?
Did he finished yet?

lessons.title: Present Perfect Continuous
lessons.explain: Use the present perfect continuous for an action that started in the past and is still going on, or that has just stopped and you can see the result. It focuses on how long. Form it with have or has been and the verb with -ing.
structures: Positive: Subject + have/has been + verb-ing: I have been waiting.
Negative: Subject + have/has not been + verb-ing: I have not been waiting.
Question: Have/Has + subject + been + verb-ing?: Have you been waiting?
positive: I have been studying English for two years.
It has been raining all morning.
They have been living here since June.
negative: I have not been sleeping well.
She has not been working lately.
questions: How long have you been waiting?
Has it been raining?
reallife: Explaining why you are tired: I have been working since six.
Asking: How long have you been learning English?

mistakes.wrong: I am waiting here since one hour.
mistakes.right: I have been waiting here for one hour.
mistakes.why: An action that started in the past and continues now needs the present perfect continuous.

mistakes.wrong: She has been know him for years.
mistakes.right: She has known him for years.
mistakes.why: State verbs like know are not used in the continuous.

exercises.prompt: I ___ been learning English since 2022. (have / has)

options: He has been work all day.
He has been working all day.
He has working all day.

exercises.prompt: How long ___ you been waiting? (have / has)
Which sentence focuses on the length of time?
options: I have been reading for two hours.
I have read two books.
I read two books.
exercises.why: The continuous form stresses the duration.

options: It has been snowing since morning.
It is snowing since morning.
It has snowing since morning.

assessment.prompt: They ___ been playing for an hour. (have / has)

options: How long have you been living here?
How long you have been living here?
How long are you living here?
I have been liking this song.
I have liked this song for years.
I am liking this song for years.
assessment.why: Like is a state verb, so use the present perfect.

lessons.title: Past Simple
lessons.explain: Use the past simple for finished actions at a definite time in the past. Regular verbs add -ed (walked). Irregular verbs have their own form (went, saw, ate). Questions and negatives use did, and the main verb goes back to the base form.
structures: Positive: Subject + past form: She visited Paris.
Negative: Subject + did not + base verb: She did not visit Paris.
Question: Did + subject + base verb?: Did she visit Paris?
positive: I watched a film last night.
We went to Goa in December.
He bought a new phone yesterday.
negative: I did not watch TV last night.
They did not go to the party.
questions: Did you see the match?
Where did you go last weekend?
reallife: Telling a story: I woke up late, missed the bus and arrived at ten.
Small talk: What did you do at the weekend?

mistakes.wrong: Did you went there?
mistakes.right: Did you go there?
mistakes.why: After did, use the base verb.

mistakes.wrong: I buyed a bag.
mistakes.right: I bought a bag.
mistakes.why: Buy is irregular: bought.

exercises.why: Went is the past of go.
After did not, use the base verb.

options: Did he came late?
Did he come late?
Does he came late?
eated
ate
eaten
exercises.why: Ate is the past simple. Eaten is the past participle.

options: We visit our aunt last Sunday.
We visited our aunt last Sunday.
We visiting our aunt last Sunday.
assessment.why: Last Sunday is finished, so use the past simple.

assessment.prompt: He ___ a book last week. (read; pronounced 'red')
assessment.why: The past of read is spelled read.

options: I didn't saw him.
I didn't see him.
I not saw him.

assessment.why: Took is the past of take.

lessons.title: Past Continuous
lessons.explain: Use the past continuous for an action that was in progress at a moment in the past, or for a longer action that was interrupted by a shorter one. Form it with was or were and the verb with -ing.
structures: Positive: Subject + was/were + verb-ing: I was cooking.
Negative: Subject + was/were not + verb-ing: I was not cooking.
Question: Was/Were + subject + verb-ing?: Were you cooking?
positive: I was sleeping at ten o'clock.
They were playing football when it started to rain.
She was reading while he was cooking.
negative: I was not working at that time.
They were not listening.
questions: What were you doing at eight?
Was he sleeping?
reallife: Explaining: I did not answer because I was driving.
Telling a story: While I was walking home, I saw an accident.

mistakes.wrong: I was cook when he called.
mistakes.right: I was cooking when he called.
mistakes.why: Was + verb-ing.

mistakes.wrong: While I walked home, I was seeing a friend.
mistakes.right: While I was walking home, I saw a friend.
mistakes.why: Use the continuous for the longer action and the simple past for the short one.

exercises.prompt: At nine last night, I ___ TV. (watch)
exercises.why: An action in progress at a moment in the past.

exercises.prompt: They ___ playing when the teacher came. (was / were)

options: When I arrived, she was cooking.
When I arrived, she cooked.
When I arrived, she is cooking.
exercises.why: The cooking was already in progress.

options: Were you sleep?
Were you sleeping?
Was you sleeping?
I was studying when the lights went out.
I studied when the lights were going out.
I was study when the lights went out.
assessment.why: Continuous for the longer action; simple for the interruption.

assessment.prompt: She ___ not listening to the teacher. (was / were)
What ___ you doing at seven? (was / were)

options: He was runing.
He was running.
He were running.
assessment.why: Run doubles the n; he + was.

assessment.prompt: While we ___ dinner, the phone rang. (have)

lessons.title: Past Perfect
lessons.explain: Use the past perfect for an action that happened before another action or time in the past. It shows which thing happened first. Form it with had and the past participle.
structures: Positive: Subject + had + past participle: I had finished.
Negative: Subject + had not + past participle: I had not finished.
Question: Had + subject + past participle?: Had you finished?
positive: When I arrived, the film had started.
She had already left when I called.
We had eaten before they came.
negative: I had not seen him before that day.
They had not finished when we arrived.
questions: Had you met her before?
Had the train left when you got there?
reallife: Explaining: I was late because I had missed the bus.
Telling a story: By the time we reached the station, the train had gone.

mistakes.wrong: When I got there, the shop already closed.
mistakes.right: When I got there, the shop had already closed.
mistakes.why: The closing happened before I got there, so use the past perfect.

mistakes.wrong: She had went home.
mistakes.right: She had gone home.
mistakes.why: Use the past participle: gone.

exercises.prompt: When we arrived, the bus ___ already left. (have / had)
Which action happened first? 'I had eaten before she came.'
options: I ate
She came
exercises.why: Had eaten is the earlier action.

exercises.prompt: He ___ never seen snow before that trip. (have / had)
exercises.why: Before a past moment, use had.

options: She had finished before I called.
She has finished before I called.
She finished had before I called.
I realised I had left my phone at home.
I realised I have left my phone at home.
I realised I had leave my phone at home.
assessment.why: The leaving happened before the realising.

assessment.prompt: By the time I got to the cinema, the film ___ started. (had / has)
assessment.why: Had started is earlier than got.

options: She had not eaten.
She not had eaten.
She had not eat.

assessment.prompt: ___ you studied before the test? (Had / Have)
assessment.why: A past reference point needs had.

assessment.prompt: They ___ already gone when I arrived. (have / had)

lessons.title: Past Perfect Continuous
lessons.explain: Use the past perfect continuous to show how long an action had been going on before another past moment, or to explain a past situation. Form it with had been and the verb with -ing.
structures: Positive: Subject + had been + verb-ing: I had been waiting.
Negative: Subject + had not been + verb-ing: I had not been waiting.
Question: Had + subject + been + verb-ing?: Had you been waiting?
positive: I had been waiting for an hour when the bus came.
She was tired because she had been working all day.
They had been living there for years before they moved.
negative: I had not been sleeping well before the exam.
He had not been working there long.
questions: How long had you been waiting?
Had it been raining?
reallife: Explaining: My eyes were red because I had been studying all night.
Telling a story: We had been walking for hours when we found the village.

mistakes.wrong: I had been wait for an hour.
mistakes.right: I had been waiting for an hour.
mistakes.why: Had been + verb-ing.

mistakes.wrong: She had been knowing him for years.
mistakes.right: She had known him for years.
mistakes.why: Know is a state verb.

exercises.prompt: He was tired because he ___ been running. (has / had)
exercises.why: The running came before the tiredness.

options: They had been playing for two hours.
They have been playing for two hours when it stopped.
They had been play for two hours.

exercises.prompt: How long ___ you been waiting before the bus came? (had / have)

options: She had been working there since 2015 when she left.
She had been worked there since 2015.
She was been working there.

assessment.prompt: I ___ been studying for three hours when you called. (had / have)
Which sentence shows duration before a past moment?
options: I had been waiting for an hour.
I waited an hour.
I am waiting for an hour.
assessment.why: The past perfect continuous shows how long.

options: Had you been practising?
Have you been practising when I arrived?
Had you been practise?

lessons.title: Future Simple
lessons.explain: Use will and the base verb for quick decisions, predictions, promises and offers. Use am, is or are going to for plans and for predictions based on what you can see now.
structures: Positive: Subject + will + base verb: I will call you.
Negative: Subject + will not (won't) + base verb: I won't be late.
Question: Will + subject + base verb?: Will you help me?
positive: I will help you with that.
It will rain tomorrow.
I am going to start a new course in May.
negative: I will not forget.
She is not going to join us.
questions: Will you be at home tonight?
What are you going to do?
reallife: Making an offer: I will carry your bag.
Promising: I will send the email today.

mistakes.wrong: I will to call you.
mistakes.right: I will call you.
mistakes.why: After will, use the base verb without to.

mistakes.wrong: If it will rain, we will stay home.
mistakes.right: If it rains, we will stay home.
mistakes.why: After if, use the present simple, not will.

exercises.prompt: The phone is ringing. You say: 'I ___ it.'
options: will answer
am answering
answered
exercises.why: A quick decision at the moment of speaking uses will.

options: She will goes tomorrow.
She will go tomorrow.
She will to go tomorrow.

exercises.prompt: Look at those clouds! It is ___ to rain. (go)
exercises.why: Going to is used when we see evidence now.

options: I will not to be late.
I won't be late.
I won't being late.

assessment.prompt: She ___ going to study medicine. (is / are)

options: If I will see him, I will tell him.
If I see him, I will tell him.
If I saw him, I will tell him.
assessment.why: After if, use the present simple.

assessment.prompt: ___ you help me move this table? (Will / Are)

options: I am going to buy a bike next month.
I will probably be tired.
It will be sunny.

lessons.title: Future Continuous
lessons.explain: Use the future continuous for an action that will be in progress at a certain time in the future. It can also politely ask about someone's plans. Form it with will be and the verb with -ing.
structures: Positive: Subject + will be + verb-ing: I will be working.
Negative: Subject + will not be + verb-ing: I will not be working.
Question: Will + subject + be + verb-ing?: Will you be working?
positive: This time tomorrow, I will be flying to Delhi.
She will be waiting for you at the station.
At eight tonight, we will be having dinner.
negative: I will not be working on Friday.
They will not be using the room.
questions: Will you be using the car tonight?
What will you be doing at nine?
reallife: Making plans: I will be travelling next week, so please email me.
Polite question: Will you be joining us for lunch?

mistakes.wrong: I will be work tomorrow evening.
mistakes.right: I will be working tomorrow evening.
mistakes.why: Will be + verb-ing.

mistakes.wrong: At six I will be knowing the result.
mistakes.right: At six I will know the result.
mistakes.why: State verbs are not used in the continuous.

exercises.prompt: This time next week, I ___ lying on a beach. (will be / am)
exercises.why: The action will be in progress at that time.

options: She will be study at nine.
She will be studying at nine.
She will studying at nine.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is a polite question about plans?
options: Will you be coming to the meeting?
Do you come to the meeting?
Did you come to the meeting?
At noon tomorrow, I will be travelling.
At noon tomorrow, I travel.
At noon tomorrow, I will travelling.

assessment.prompt: They ___ be sleeping at midnight. (will / are)

options: I will not be working tomorrow.
I will be not working tomorrow.
I will not working tomorrow.

assessment.prompt: What ___ you be doing this time tomorrow? (will / are)
She will be ___ at the airport. (wait)

lessons.title: Future Perfect
lessons.explain: Use the future perfect for an action that will be finished before a certain time in the future. It often goes with by and by the time. Form it with will have and the past participle.
structures: Positive: Subject + will have + past participle: I will have finished.
Negative: Subject + will not have + past participle: I will not have finished.
Question: Will + subject + have + past participle?: Will you have finished?
positive: By Friday, I will have finished the report.
She will have graduated by next June.
By the time you arrive, we will have eaten.
negative: I will not have finished by five.
They will not have arrived by noon.
questions: Will you have finished by six?
How many pages will you have written?
reallife: At work: I will have sent the invoice by the end of the day.
Planning: By next year, I will have saved enough money.

mistakes.wrong: I will have finish by Friday.
mistakes.right: I will have finished by Friday.
mistakes.why: Will have + past participle.

mistakes.wrong: By the time you come, I will finish.
mistakes.right: By the time you come, I will have finished.
mistakes.why: The action is completed before the future time.

exercises.prompt: By next month, I ___ have saved £500. (will / would)

options: She will have left by nine.
She will has left by nine.
She will have leave by nine.

exercises.prompt: They will have ___ the project by Monday. (finish)
Which sentence shows a completed future action?
options: By 2030, I will have learned Spanish.
In 2030, I will learn Spanish.
I am learning Spanish.
exercises.why: By + a future time with the future perfect.

options: By the time you arrive, I will have cooked dinner.
By the time you arrive, I will cook dinner.
By the time you arrive, I will have cook dinner.
assessment.why: The cooking finishes before you arrive.

options: Will you have finished by noon?
Will you finished by noon?
Have you will finished by noon?

assessment.prompt: We will have ___ the house by June. (sell)
assessment.why: Sold is the past participle of sell.

assessment.prompt: I won't have ___ the report by five. (write)
assessment.why: Written is the past participle of write.

lessons.title: Future Perfect Continuous
lessons.explain: Use the future perfect continuous to show how long an action will have been going on at a point in the future. It stresses the length of time. Form it with will have been and the verb with -ing.
structures: Positive: Subject + will have been + verb-ing: I will have been working.
Negative: Subject + will not have been + verb-ing: I will not have been working.
Question: Will + subject + have been + verb-ing?: Will you have been working?
positive: By June, I will have been learning English for three years.
Next month, she will have been working here for a decade.
By six o'clock, they will have been driving for eight hours.
negative: I will not have been working there long.
She will not have been studying for a year.
questions: How long will you have been living here by then?
Will they have been waiting long?
reallife: At work: By December, I will have been working here for five years.
Planning: By the time we arrive, we will have been travelling for ten hours.

mistakes.wrong: By June I will have been learn English for two years.
mistakes.right: By June I will have been learning English for two years.
mistakes.why: Will have been + verb-ing.

mistakes.wrong: By then I will have been knowing her for ten years.
mistakes.right: By then I will have known her for ten years.
mistakes.why: Know is a state verb.

exercises.prompt: By May, I ___ have been working here for a year. (will / would)

options: She will have been teaching for ten years.
She will have teaching for ten years.
She will be have teaching for ten years.

exercises.prompt: By noon, we will have been ___ for four hours. (drive)
What does this tense usually stress?
options: The length of an action up to a future time
A quick decision
A finished past action
exercises.why: It shows duration up to a point in the future.

options: By 2030, he will have been living here for ten years.
By 2030, he will have lived been here.
By 2030, he will been living here.

assessment.prompt: They will have been ___ for two hours by then. (wait)

options: How long will you have been studying by June?
How long will you been studying by June?
How long you will have been studying by June?

assessment.prompt: She ___ not have been working long. (will / has)

options: By next week, I will have been practising for a month.
By next week, I have been practising for a month.
By next week, I will practising for a month.
assessment.why: Future perfect continuous shows duration up to a future time.
